Yellowfin madtom (Noturus flavipinnis) is a small, imperiled ictalurid catfish endemic to upland streams of the upper Tennessee River drainage, and a growing body of field research has begun to illuminate its life-history parameters. Reproductive females deposit adhesive, demersal eggs within cryptic nest cavities, and based on the measured egg diameter of 2.8 millimeters, which yields a calculated spherical volume, the resultant wet weight at birth for newly hatched yolk-sac larvae is approximately 0.0115 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0115 grams]. This modest initial mass is typical of small-bodied lotic ictalurids and necessitates a period of rapid endogenous yolk absorption before the onset of exogenous feeding. Field surveys of nesting individuals indicate that under stable thermal regimes, a single female may produce a clutch of roughly 60 to 80 eggs per nesting event [N_R_i = roughly 60 to 80 eggs per nesting event], with most reproductively active adults spawning approximately 2 to 3 times per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 times per year], a rate that is constrained by the availability of suitable undercut banks and slab-rock refugia. The product of these values yields a maximum daily reproduction rate of roughly 180 offspring per year [Ri = roughly 180 offspring per year], consistent with the species' reproductive capacity at 20 °C [T = 20 °C].

Individual growth proceeds slowly in the oligotrophic headwater reaches, and available mark-recapture data indicate that females reach the standard length at puberty at approximately 7.5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 7.5 centimeters]. This milestone typically occurs after two growing seasons and marks the onset of vitellogenesis and gonadal recrudescence in sexually maturing females. The attainment of this size threshold is strongly temperature-dependent, with individuals inhabiting cooler, spring-fed tributaries often delaying maturation relative to conspecifics in more thermally variable mainstem sections. Comparative studies of related madtom species suggest that a standard length at puberty of 7.5 cm represents a moderate value within the genus, reflecting the species’ adaptation to stable, low-productivity environments. After reaching puberty, females appear to allocate a substantial proportion of somatic surplus toward egg production, although the trade-off between growth and reproduction results in only modest annual fecundity compared to larger-bodied ictalurids.

Longitudinal studies of captive-reared cohorts maintained at a constant water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have provided valuable insights into the species’ maximal physiological capacity. Under these controlled conditions, the maximum recorded reproductive rate, expressed as the product of clutch size and spawning frequency, equates to approximately 0.49 offspring per day per individual, though this rate is rarely sustained in wild populations due to resource limitation and nest predation. The reproductive output is partitioned into a multiple annual clutches for most females, and the daily equivalent underscores the relatively low fecundity of this specialist compared to more fecund, broadcast-spawning cyprinids. The highest observed feeding rates in these captive trials occurred during the pre-spawning period, when females actively foraged on benthic macroinvertebrates to support oocyte development. These experimental data complement field observations of nest-guarding behavior and egg survival rates in natural stream environments.

The ultimate standard length recorded for this species is 15 centimeters [Li = 15 centimeters], a size achieved by only the oldest and largest individuals in the most productive stream reaches. This maximum length is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 25.4 grams [Wwi = 25.4 grams], estimated from length-weight regressions developed for this species and corroborated by dissections of large-bodied museum specimens. Fish approaching this asymptotic size display a markedly reduced growth rate, with annual increments of less than one centimeter in standard length, indicating that energetic resources are increasingly diverted toward maintenance and reproductive functions rather than somatic expansion. The allometric relationship between length and weight follows a positive power function typical of benthic stream fishes, and the 25.4 gram maximum mass places the yellowfin madtom among the larger members of the subgenus Rabida. Such large individuals are disproportionately important to population persistence due to their elevated fecundity.

Comprehensive demographic analyses conducted at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] indicate that the maximum documented life span for Noturus flavipinnis in both wild and captive settings is 4 years [am = 4 years], after which senescence-related mortality increases sharply. This relatively short life span, which places the species among the shorter-lived Ictaluridae comparable to Noturus exilis, is typical of small-bodied ictalurids and is coupled with a semelparous or weak iteroparous reproductive strategy, whereby most females complete only one or two spawning seasons before dying. The oldest individuals, those reaching age four, are rarely encountered in population surveys, representing less than five percent of the adult population in most years. Mortality rates are highest during the first year of life, driven by predation from larger centrarchids and sculpins as well as by seasonal low-flow events that reduce suitable foraging habitat. Understanding the interplay between this 4-year longevity (4 years) [am = 4 years] and the species’ low annual fecundity of roughly 180 offspring per year [Ri = roughly 180 offspring per year] under a constant thermal regime of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] is critical for effective conservation planning, as population recovery following disturbance is inherently slow.
